opening_question_spark: Why does one tune loop while you sort tools, even after the music stops?
book_transition: The answer starts with how memory handles sound.

body: Scientists call this involuntary musical imagery, or an earworm.
Recent or repeated listening can trigger it.
Short, distinctive fragments are easy to retrieve.
Repetition makes the next note feel predictable.
Your brain can replay that pattern without sound.
Idle moments give the loop room to return.
Mood and personal memories can strengthen the cue.
Fighting it can keep your attention locked on it.
An absorbing task can redirect that attention.
Then the loop often fades on its own.
optional_closing: The music stopped, but the pattern kept moving.
full_narration: Why does one tune loop while you sort tools, even after the music stops? The answer starts with how memory handles sound. Scientists call this involuntary musical imagery, or an earworm. Recent or repeated listening can trigger it. Short, distinctive fragments are easy to retrieve. Repetition makes the next note feel predictable. Your brain can replay that pattern without sound. Idle moments give the loop room to return. Mood and personal memories can strengthen the cue. Fighting it can keep your attention locked on it. An absorbing task can redirect that attention. Then the loop often fades on its own. The music stopped, but the pattern kept moving.
